meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem to form a compound verb. It means finishing or completing something, or an action directed upward.
connection: Verb masu-stem + 上げる (intransitive form: 〜上がる)

senses.label: Finish, complete
senses.meaning: Doing something that takes time and effort all the way to the end, and producing a finished result. There is a sense of accomplishment: “finally done”. Like English “finish ...ing” or “... up”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 上げる (書き上げる・作り上げる・仕上げる・育て上げる・磨き上げる)
examples: I spent three days and finished writing the report.
We all worked together to create a single piece of work.
My mother raised three children all on her own.

senses.label: Upward
senses.meaning: The action goes upward. This keeps the original meaning of 「上げる」, “to raise”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 上げる (見上げる・持ち上げる・積み上げる・引き上げる)
examples: When I looked up at the night sky, the stars were beautiful.
This box is so heavy that I can't lift it by myself.

senses.label: Polite, humble
senses.meaning: A few words have become fixed humble or formal expressions. 「申し上げる」 is the humble form of 「言う」, and 「存じ上げる」 is the humble form of 「知る」.
senses.connection: 申し上げる・存じ上げる (mostly in business and formal settings)
examples: I thank you from the bottom of my heart.
I have known your name for a long time.

notes: 「〜上げる」 attaches to the masu-stem, while 「〜てあげる」 attaches to the te-form. One small difference, a completely different meaning: 「書き上げた」 means “I finished writing it”, but 「書いてあげた」 means “I wrote it for someone”.
「申し上げる」 and 「存じ上げる」 are humble expressions and can only describe actions by you or your side. Using them for a superior is very rude: ✕「社長が申し上げました」→ ○「社長がおっしゃいました」.
The “completion” meaning only works with effortful actions that produce a finished result. For simply finishing an ordinary action, use 「〜終わる」: ✕「ご飯を食べ上げた」→ ○「ご飯を食べ終わった」.
Don't confuse transitive 「〜上げる」 with intransitive 「〜上がる」: ✕「料理が作り上げた」→ ○「料理を作り上げた」／「料理が出来上がった」.

daily.title: Finishing an assignment
daily.description: A student tells a friend the work is finally done.
daily.example: I finally finished writing my graduation thesis!

daily.title: Talking about cooking
daily.description: Saying you took your time to finish a dish.
daily.example: I slowly simmered the curry until it was done.

daily.title: Helping with a move
daily.description: Two people lifting something heavy together.
daily.example: Let's lift it together on three.

work.title: Formal greeting
work.description: Politely expressing thanks or regards in a business email or speech.
work.example: We look forward to your continued support.

work.title: Project finished
work.description: Reporting to a boss that a document is ready.
work.example: I finished the proposal this morning.

etymology: 「上げる」 originally means “to lift something up, to raise”. As the second part of a compound, “upward” came to mean “reaching the top”, and then “doing it to the end, completing”. The humble 「申し上げる」 comes from “presenting” words up to a person of higher status.

similar.title: 〜終わる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜終わる」 just states objectively that an action ended, and works with almost any verb (「読み終わる」, 「食べ終わる」). 「〜上げる」 stresses that effort went into producing a finished piece, and is mostly used for writing, making, and raising (「書き上げる」, 「育て上げる」).

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜切る」 stresses “all of it, nothing left” (「使い切る」), or a state reaching its extreme (「疲れ切る」). 「〜上げる」 stresses bringing a piece of work to a complete, finished form, with no sense of “using up”.

similar.title: 〜お〜申し上げる・ご〜申し上げる
similar.explanation: Same origin: these also use 「上げる」 in the sense of “offering up”. 「お／ご〜申し上げる」 is a humble pattern for doing something for a superior (「ご案内申し上げます」); the 「申し上げる」 in this entry is a humble verb that has become fixed within it.

formation: 「〜上げる」 = verb masu-stem + the transitive verb 「上げる」 (to raise, to lift). The first verb names the concrete action, and 「上げる」 gives it an upward direction. When the action itself literally goes up, you get 「見上げる」 and 「持ち上げる」. Read “upward” as “piling up all the way to the top”, and you get the meaning “carry through to the end, produce a finished piece”: 「書き上げる」 is building a text up bit by bit until it is complete. Because it means piling up to the top, it mostly pairs with time-consuming, effortful actions that yield a product. “Raising up” words or feelings to someone of higher status gives humble expressions like 「申し上げる」 and 「存じ上げる」. The intransitive 「上がる」 works the same way to form 「出来上がる」, meaning something gets completed on its own.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. Two or more people do the same action to each other, or do something together.
connection: Verb masu-stem + 合う (noun form: 〜合い)

senses.label: Each other
senses.meaning: Both sides do the same thing to each other: “... each other”. The subject is plural, or uses 「AとBが」 or 「お互いに」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 合う (助け合う・励まし合う・見つめ合う・愛し合う)
examples: Let's help each other when we're in trouble.
The two of them were silently gazing at each other.
The team members practiced while encouraging one another.

senses.label: Together
senses.meaning: Several people do something together, with exchange and sharing between them, as in discussing, sharing, or talking.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 合う (話し合う・分け合う・語り合う・意見を出し合う)
examples: Let's all talk this problem over and decide.
The three of us shared one cake.
I talked with an old friend until morning.

notes: 「〜合う」 requires both sides to do the same action to each other. One-directional actions can't use it: ✕「先輩が私を助け合った」→ ○「先輩が私を助けてくれた」／「私たちは助け合った」.
The partner in the mutual action is marked with 「と」, not 「を」: ✕「彼を見つめ合った」→ ○「彼と見つめ合った」.
In 「似合う」 (to suit), 「間に合う」 (to be in time), and 「気が合う」 (to get along), 「合う」 means “to match” and has nothing to do with “each other”: 「この服は彼に似合う」 does not mean “...each other”.
「話し合う」 means both sides discuss something together. 「打ち合わせ」 (a planning meeting) and 「待ち合わせ」 (meeting up at an agreed place) come from 「合わせる」 and differ in both meaning and usage.

daily.title: Dividing chores
daily.description: A family discusses how to split the housework.
daily.example: We talked over how to divide up the housework.

daily.title: Between friends
daily.description: Saying you and your friend help and support each other.
daily.example: My friend and I can talk to each other about anything.

daily.title: Introducing someone
daily.description: Introducing a person you know.
daily.example: He's someone I know from college.

work.title: Teamwork
work.description: A manager asks the department to work together.
work.example: It's important for departments to share information with one another.

work.title: Meeting discussion
work.description: Suggesting in a meeting that everyone share ideas.
work.example: First, let's all freely put our ideas on the table.

etymology: 「合う」 originally means “two things come together, match”. After a verb, it shows actions coming from both sides and “meeting” in the middle, which gives the sense of “each other, together”.

similar.title: 〜に合わせて・〜に合った
similar.explanation: Same origin: also from 「合う」; the transitive 「合わせる」 means “to make things match”. 「〜に合わせて」 is adjusting yourself to a standard (「音楽に合わせて踊る」), while 「〜合う」 is both sides doing the same action to each other (「手を取り合って踊る」).

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜とともに」 means “together with” and only states that people act jointly; it has a fairly written tone. 「〜合う」 stresses an action going back and forth between both sides. 「友達とともに勉強する」 is studying together; 「友達と教え合う」 is teaching each other.

formation: 「〜合う」 = verb masu-stem + 「合う」 (two things come together, match). Picture 「合う」 as two things approaching from either side and meeting in the middle. Attached to a verb, it turns the action into something both sides direct at each other at the same time, meeting in the middle, which gives the meaning “each other”: 「助け合う」 = you help me, I help you. When there are more than two participants, the actions weave together among everyone, giving the meaning “together, jointly”: 「話し合う」, 「分け合う」. Precisely because the action must “meet” between both sides, one-directional actions can't use 「〜合う」, and the partner is marked with 「と」, the particle for a co-participant.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. It means doing an action completely, a state reaching its extreme, or acting decisively; the negative 「〜切れない」 means being unable to finish it all or to do it thoroughly.
connection: Verb ます-stem + きる／きれる／きれない (also written 「切る」)

senses.label: Do completely
senses.meaning: Carrying an action through to the end with nothing left over: “... it all up, ... to the end”. Often used with 「全部」 or 「最後まで」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 切る (使い切る・食べ切る・読み切る・走り切る)
examples: I used up my whole salary in a month.
I read this entire novel in one night.
I ran the marathon all the way to the end.

senses.label: Totally, extremely
senses.meaning: A state reaches its peak: “completely, utterly”. Often with state verbs such as 「疲れる」, 「冷える」, and 「困る」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 切る／切った (疲れ切る・冷え切る・困り切る・分かり切ったこと)
examples: By the time I got home from work, I was completely exhausted.
That's perfectly obvious.
My body got chilled to the bone.

senses.label: Decisively
senses.meaning: Doing something firmly, without hesitation, as in 「言い切る」 (declare) and 「思い切る」 (make up one's mind).
senses.connection: 言い切る・思い切って・割り切る・押し切る
examples: He declared, “We'll definitely win.”
I worked up the courage and confessed my feelings to her.

senses.label: Can't finish
senses.meaning: There is too much to get through it all: “can't finish ..., too many to ...”. Often with 「多すぎて」 or 「とても」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 切れない (食べ切れない・数え切れない・持ち切れない)
examples: There's too much food. I can't eat it all.
There were countless stars in the night sky.
I had so much luggage that I couldn't carry it all by myself.

senses.label: Can't fully
senses.meaning: You can't do something completely, emotionally or in ability: “can't quite ..., can't bring yourself to ...”. Often with 「諦める」, 「待つ」, 「我慢する」, 「言う」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + きれない (諦めきれない・待ちきれない・我慢しきれない・言い切れない)
examples: I just can't give up on my dream.
I can't wait for tomorrow's trip.
I can't say for sure that he's the culprit.

notes: For simply finishing something, use 「〜終わる」; 「〜切る」 stresses “all of it, nothing left”: 「ご飯を食べ終わった」 means you finished your meal, while 「大盛りを全部食べ切った」 means you ate the whole large portion down to the last bite.

「言い切る」 means “to state flatly, to declare”, and 「思い切る」 means “to make up your mind, to go for it”. Neither means “finish saying” or “finish thinking”: 「思い切って告白した」 means you worked up the courage to confess.
When you want to do something but can't finish it, use the negative potential 「〜切れない」. 「〜切らない」 only means “didn't do all of it”: 「多すぎて食べ切れない」 (too much to finish), never ✕「多すぎて食べ切らない」.

「〜とは言い切れない」 is a soft, partial negation meaning “you can't say for certain that...”, not “it is definitely not”: 「彼が悪いとは言い切れない」 means “you can't say it's definitely his fault”, which is not the same as “he did nothing wrong”.
「待ちきれない」 means “can't wait, eagerly looking forward to it”. It expresses excitement, not “can't keep waiting, about to give up”: 「明日の旅行が待ちきれない」.

daily.title: Clearing out the fridge
daily.description: Wanting to use up food before it expires.
daily.example: Let's finish the milk before the best-before date.

daily.title: Home from work
daily.description: Telling your family you're worn out.
daily.example: I'm really exhausted today.

daily.title: Working up courage
daily.description: A friend talks about making a bold decision.
daily.example: I took the plunge and cut my hair short.

daily.title: Looking forward
daily.description: A child is excited about the amusement park.
daily.example: I can't wait for the weekend!

daily.title: Too much food
daily.description: Telling friends you ordered too much.
daily.example: If we order this much, we won't be able to finish it.

work.title: Budget management
work.description: Accounting notes the yearly budget is gone.
work.example: We have already used up this fiscal year's budget.

work.title: Final push
work.description: A manager encourages the team to see it through.
work.example: Let's see this through to the end.

work.title: Too much work
work.description: Telling your boss you can't handle it alone.
work.example: I can't process this volume on my own.

work.title: Careful judgment
work.description: Avoiding absolute conclusions in a report.
work.example: We cannot say for certain that there is only one cause.

etymology: From the verb 「切る」 (to cut). “Cut all the way through” became “finish completely, reach the limit”. As an auxiliary verb it is usually written in kana: 「きる」.
formation: 「〜切る」 = verb masu-stem + 「切る」 (to cut off). The core image of 「切る」 is “cut clean through and be done with it”. After an action verb, it means carrying the action all the way to the point where it is “cut off”, with nothing left to do, which gives the meaning “finish all of it”: 「使い切る」 = use until nothing remains. After a verb of changing state, it means the state has advanced to its end and can go no further, which gives “completely, extremely”: 「疲れ切る」, 「冷え切る」. Cutting off your words or thoughts with no room left gives 「言い切る」 (to declare) and 「思い切る」 (to make up your mind). All three meanings revolve around the single image of “cutting off, leaving no room”. 「〜切れない」 is its negative potential form (「〜切る」→「〜切れる」→「〜切れない」), meaning “cannot carry it through”: with quantities, something is left over and it cannot be finished (「食べ切れない」「数え切れない」); with feelings, part of the mind still holds back (「諦め切れない」「待ちきれない」). So it negates “thoroughness”, not the action itself.

similar.title: 〜終わる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜終わる」 just states objectively that an action ended; 「〜切る」 stresses doing all of it, thoroughly. 「本を読み終わった」 just means you finished reading, while 「厚い本を一晩で読み切った」 stresses reading that whole thick book in one go.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜抜く」 stresses overcoming difficulty and persisting to the end (「最後まで走り抜く」), focusing on the hardship of the process. 「〜切る」 focuses on the result of finishing everything with nothing left (「42キロを走り切る」).

similar.title: 〜尽くす
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜尽くす」 also means “nothing left”, but is more literary and stresses exhausting or covering everything within a range (「食べ尽くす」, 「知り尽くす」). 「〜切る」 is used much more widely and can also express a state at its extreme (「疲れ切る」), which 「〜尽くす」 cannot.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “hard to do”. 「〜かねる」 means you can't do it because of your position or circumstances, and is often used to decline politely (「お答えしかねます」). 「〜切れない」 means you can't finish or can't do it completely because there is too much or it doesn't go far enough. When politely declining a client, use 「〜かねます」, not 「〜切れません」.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ようがない」 means “there's no way to do it, no place to start”, because the means are missing (「連絡先が分からないので連絡しようがない」). 「〜切れない」 means you can do it but can't finish or can't do it completely (「星が多くて数え切れない」).

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. It means going into a place, putting something in, or an action or state going deep and continuing.
connection: Verb masu-stem + 込む (noun form: 〜込み)

senses.label: Into, in
senses.meaning: Moving from outside to inside, or putting something inside: “... into, ... in”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 込む (入り込む・飛び込む・持ち込む・書き込む・詰め込む)
examples: A child jumped into the river.
Please refrain from bringing in drinks.
I crammed my things into my bag.

senses.label: Deeply, thoroughly
senses.meaning: An action or state goes deep, becomes thorough, and lasts a while: “deep in ..., ... thoroughly”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 込む (考え込む・黙り込む・煮込む・思い込む・落ち込む)
examples: He has his arms folded, lost in thought.
I failed the exam and got really down.
Simmer the meat slowly over low heat.

senses.label: Set vocabulary
senses.meaning: Some words have their own fixed meaning and are best learned as a whole: 「申し込む」 (apply, sign up), 「振り込む」 (transfer money), 「冷え込む」 (get very cold).
senses.connection: 申し込む・振り込む・冷え込む・売り込む
examples: I signed up for a cooking class.
Please transfer the payment to our bank account.

notes: 「落ち込む」 mainly means “to feel down, be depressed” (it can also mean figures dropping), and 「思い込む」 means “to be convinced (often mistakenly)”. Don't read them literally as “fall into” or “think into”.

「〜込む」 adds a sense of “burrowing in, going deep” to the original verb, so the two can't be swapped freely: 「部屋に入る」 is just entering, while 「部屋に入り込む」 suggests slipping in or intruding without permission (「泥棒が入り込んだ」).
A sign in a shop saying 「お持ち込みはご遠慮ください」 means “please do not bring in outside food or drink”. In Japan, bringing outside food into a shop to eat it is considered rude.
When 「込む」 stands alone meaning “crowded”, it is usually written 「混む」: 「電車が混んでいる」. Only 「〜込む」 after a verb masu-stem is this pattern.

daily.title: Catching a train
daily.description: Someone rushes onto the train.
daily.example: A man dashed in right before the train left.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is down after a failure.
daily.example: Don't be so down.

daily.title: Cold weather
daily.description: Commenting on the sudden cold in the morning.
daily.example: It got really cold this morning, didn't it?

work.title: Payment notice
work.description: A company asks a customer to pay by the deadline.
work.example: Please make the bank transfer by the end of the month.

work.title: Filling out a form
work.description: A receptionist explains how to fill in a form.
work.example: Please fill in the required items here. Once you've filled it in, please hand it in.

etymology: 「込む」 originally means “to fill up, pack in; to be crowded”. As the second part of a compound, it means “moving inward”. From going deep in space, it extended to going deep in mind or degree: “deeply, thoroughly”.

similar.title: 〜を込めて
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「込める」 is the transitive counterpart of 「込む」. 「〜を込めて」 follows a noun and means putting feelings or effort “into” something (「心を込めて書く」); this pattern follows a verb masu-stem and means an action going inside or going deep.

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: often compared when describing states: 「冷え込む」 is cold settling in step by step (usually about the weather getting colder), while 「冷え切る」 is being chilled through, to the extreme (「体が冷え切った」). 「〜込む」 focuses on the process of going deeper; 「〜切る」 on the result of reaching the limit.

similar.title: 〜続ける
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「考え込む」 is being lost in thought and unable to get out, while 「考え続ける」 is just objectively continuing to think. 「〜込む」 stresses being sunk deep in it; 「〜続ける」 stresses uninterrupted continuation in time.

formation: 「〜込む」 = verb masu-stem + 「込む」 (to pack in, to fill). The core image of 「込む」 is “going into the inside, filling up the inside”. After verbs of moving or placing, the action heads inward: 「飛び込む」 (jump in), 「詰め込む」 (cram in). Shift that “inward” from space to time and the mind, and it means an action going deep and staying sunk in it: 「考え込む」, 「煮込む」, 「落ち込む」. So 「〜込む」 adds a sense of direction, “deeper, inward”, to the original verb. Through heavy use, many of these words have become fixed with new meanings (「申し込む」 to apply, 「振り込む」 to transfer money).

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. You redo an action because you weren't satisfied with it or there was a mistake.
connection: Verb masu-stem + 直す (noun form: 〜直し)

senses.label: Redo, correct
senses.meaning: Doing something again because it was poor or wrong, to make it better: “re-..., ... over again”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 直す (書き直す・やり直す・作り直す・言い直す)
examples: Your handwriting is messy, so please rewrite it.
Even if you fail, you can start over as many times as you want.
Sorry, let me rephrase that.

senses.label: Reconsider
senses.meaning: Thinking about or looking at something again, and changing your view or decision. 「見直す」 can also mean “see someone in a new, better light”.
senses.connection: 見直す・考え直す・読み直す・問い直す
examples: Let's check it over once more before submitting.
I reconsidered studying abroad.
When I saw an unexpected side of him, my opinion of him went up.

senses.label: Do again
senses.meaning: Not necessarily because of a mistake; just doing it once more, such as calling back or coming back another time.
senses.connection: かけ直す・出直す・入れ直す
examples: I'll call you back later.
It looks like nobody's home today, so let's come back tomorrow.

notes: 「見直す」 has two meanings: “to re-examine, revise” and “to see someone in a new, better light”. 「彼を見直した」 means you've come to think more highly of him (a compliment), not that you looked at him again.

「〜直す」 implies “the first attempt wasn't good and needs fixing”. Saying 「やり直してください」 or 「書き直してください」 directly to a superior or client amounts to telling them their work wasn't good enough, which is very rude. Instead, you can say 「お手数ですが、こちらをご確認いただけますか」.
When you simply do something once more with no sense of correcting it, use 「もう一度〜」: ✕「おいしかったので、もう一回食べ直した」→ ○「おいしかったので、もう一度食べた」.
「出直す」 means “to come back another time; to start over”, and 「かけ直す」 means “to call again, call back”. Both are common fixed expressions.

daily.title: A missed call
daily.description: Saying you'll call back when it's a bad time.
daily.example: I'm driving right now, so I'll call you back later.

daily.title: Exam review
daily.description: A student checks the answers.
daily.example: I went over all my answers, but I'm still nervous.

work.title: Revising a document
work.description: A boss asks for a report to be redone.
work.example: Please redo this part with the data included.

work.title: Adjusting a plan
work.description: Proposing in a meeting to review the plan.
work.example: We need to review the plan in terms of cost.

work.title: Returning a call
work.description: An operator tells a customer they'll get a call back.
work.example: I'll have the person in charge call you back.

etymology: 「直す」 originally means “to make straight, to fix”. After a verb, it means “fixing” an action you already did, that is, doing it over.

similar.title: 〜てみる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (often compared): 「考えてみる」 means “try thinking about it”, without rejecting any earlier result; 「考え直す」 means throwing out your original idea and reconsidering. 「もう一度やってみる」 is giving it another try, while 「やり直す」 is starting over because you failed or weren't satisfied.

formation: 「〜直す」 = verb masu-stem + 「直す」 (to set right, to fix). The core of 「直す」 is “straightening out what is crooked or broken”. Attached to a verb, the thing being fixed becomes the preceding action itself: 「書き直す」 = rewriting something badly written so it comes out right. So 「〜直す」 naturally carries the premise that the previous attempt was unsatisfactory or wrong, and this is what sets it apart from simply doing something again. Fixing your “view” of something gives 「見直す」, both “re-examine” and “see someone in a new light”; redoing a “visit” gives 「出直す」 (come back another time).

meaning: Follows the verb masu-stem: an action is half done, something is about to happen, or an action is directed at someone.
connection: Verb masu-stem + かける／かけだ／かけの + noun

senses.label: Half done
senses.meaning: An action has started but stopped partway and isn't finished. Common forms: 「〜かけの + noun」, 「〜かけた」, 「〜かけて (やめる)」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + かけの + noun／かけて (食べかけ・読みかけ・言いかけて)
examples: A half-read book is lying on the desk.
He started to say something, then stopped.
Don't throw away the half-eaten bread.

senses.label: About to, almost
senses.meaning: A state is about to happen or has begun to appear, but isn't complete: “almost ..., nearly ...”. Often with 「死ぬ」, 「忘れる」, 「壊れる」.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + かける／かけている (死にかける・忘れかける・壊れかける)
examples: As a child, I once nearly drowned in a river.
I remembered a dream I had almost forgotten.
This chair is about to fall apart.

senses.label: Directed at someone
senses.meaning: With 「話す」, 「呼ぶ」, 「笑う」 and so on, the action is “aimed” at another person: “speak to, call on”.
senses.connection: 話しかける・呼びかける・問いかける・笑いかける・働きかける
examples: A stranger spoke to me at the station.
They are calling on citizens to save electricity.

notes: 「死にかけた」 and 「溺れかけた」 mean “nearly... (but didn't)”. The outcome never actually happened, so don't take it to mean the person died.
「言いかけてやめた」 is different from 「言おうとしてやめた」: in the first, you had already said part of it and stopped mid-sentence; in the second, not a single word had come out yet.
In 「話しかける」, 「呼びかける」, and 「問いかける」, 「かける」 means “to direct at someone” and has nothing to do with “halfway”: 「知らない人に話しかけられた」 means a stranger started talking to you.
「出かける」, 「見かける」, and 「追いかける」 are now independent verbs; they don't mean “halfway out” or “halfway through looking”.
To modify a noun use 「〜かけの＋noun」: ✕「食べかけるパン」→ ○「食べかけのパン」.

daily.title: Tidying up
daily.description: Seeing leftover food on the table.
daily.example: Put away your half-eaten snacks, OK?

daily.title: Talking about the past
daily.description: Mentioning something you'd almost forgotten.
daily.example: I'd almost forgotten about that.

daily.title: A close call
daily.description: Telling a friend about almost drowning.
daily.example: When I was a kid, I nearly drowned in a river.

daily.title: Making friends
daily.description: Saying you spoke to a new classmate first.
daily.example: I worked up the courage and talked to the person next to me.

work.title: Unfinished work
work.description: Explaining progress during a handover.
work.example: I'll continue the half-finished work tomorrow.

work.title: Public notice
work.description: A government or company appeals to the public.
work.example: They are urging people to watch out for heatstroke.

work.title: Handing over work
work.description: Before leaving, telling a coworker your work isn't finished.
work.example: There's a half-written email left in my drafts.

etymology: 「かける」 (掛ける) originally means “to hang, to put on”. As the second part of a compound, it means “putting an action on”, just getting a start on it. This gives “half done” and “about to”. The “directed at someone” use comes from “throwing an action toward someone”.
formation: 「〜かける」 = verb masu-stem + 「かける」 (掛ける: to hang on, to hook onto). The core of 「かける」 is “catching hold, just barely touching”. After a verb, it means the action has just “caught hold” of its beginning, started but not finished, which gives the meaning “halfway through”. The noun form 「〜かけ」 describes that half-done state (「飲みかけのコーヒー」). For verbs of change, “just catching hold” means the change has begun and is about to take shape, which gives “about to, nearly” (「死にかける」). “Hanging” an action onto another person gives the meaning “directed at someone” (「話しかける」, 「呼びかける」).

similar.title: 〜そうになる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can mean “nearly...”. 「〜そうになる」 only says something was about to happen but in the end didn't (「転びそうになった」); 「〜かける」 often implies the situation had already started to unfold (「死にかけた」 means you were once on the brink of death).

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとする
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ようとする」 is intentionally being “about to do” something, before the action has started (「言おうとした」). 「〜かける」 means the action had started and stopped partway (「言いかけた」).

similar.title: 〜途中で・〜途中に
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜途中で」 objectively states that something is in the middle of a process and works with movement and events (「帰る途中で」, 「会議の途中で」). 「〜かけ（の）」 stresses that an action was left half done, and often modifies objects (「読みかけの本」).

similar.title: 〜ところだった
similar.explanation: 「〜ところだった」 means “almost ... (luckily not),” where the event didn't happen at all (「遅れるところだった」); 「〜かけた」 means the change had already begun to occur in part.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. You keep doing something from start to finish without giving up.
connection: Verb masu-stem + 通す (noun form: 〜通し)

senses.label: See it through
senses.meaning: Overcoming difficulty and carrying a will or action through to the end: “see ... through, stick with ...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 通す (やり通す・守り通す・貫き通す・隠し通す)
examples: Once I've decided something, I want to see it through to the end.
He kept the secret right to the end.
It's hard to keep up a lie all the way.

senses.label: Start to finish
senses.meaning: Going through a distance, a book, etc. from beginning to end without stopping: “... all the way through, in one go”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 通す (読み通す・走り通す・歩き通す)
examples: I read a thick novel straight through in one go.
I walked all the way to the summit without a break.

senses.label: Nonstop (〜通し)
senses.meaning: The noun form 「〜通しだ」 shows a state continuing with no break: “... the whole time, nonstop”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 通しだ／通しで (立ち通し・働き通し・笑い通し)
examples: I was standing the whole hour on a packed train.
I worked nonstop from morning till night, and I'm tired.

notes: 「見通す」 means “to see through, to foresee” (the noun 「見通し」 means outlook or prospects), not “to keep watching”: ✕「三時間テレビを見通した」→ ○「三時間テレビを見続けた」.

「〜通す」 stresses not giving up midway and carrying something through to the end. For mere continuation in time, use 「〜続ける」: 「走り続けた」 may have stopped somewhere, while 「走り通した」 means you ran the entire course.
「嘘をつき通す」, 「隠し通す」, and 「黙り通す」 are also common and mean “keep it hidden to the very end”, so the pattern is not always positive.
In 「目を通す」 (to look over) and 「客を部屋に通す」 (to show a guest into a room), 「通す」 is used on its own and is not this pattern.

daily.title: Sticking to a diet
daily.description: A friend vows to stick with a plan.
daily.example: This time I'm going to stick with my diet to the end.

daily.title: Standing all the way
daily.description: Complaining after work about standing on the train.
daily.example: I had to stand the whole way home on the train.

work.title: Owning a project
work.description: A manager tells a staff member to see a project through.
work.example: Please take responsibility and see your assigned work through.

work.title: Negotiations
work.description: News reports one side sticking to its position.
work.example: The company pushed its position through to the end.

etymology: 「通す」 originally means “to pass through, to pierce through”. As the second part of a compound, it means an action runs through from one end to the other, so it means “from start to finish, to the end”.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean persisting to the end. 「〜抜く」 stresses overcoming difficulty and going to the utmost (「考え抜く」, 「戦い抜く」); 「〜通す」 stresses keeping the same attitude from start to finish without change (「守り通す」, 「黙り通す」).

similar.title: 〜続ける
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜続ける」 only expresses continuation in time, whether or not the end is reached; 「〜通す」 stresses doing it all the way to the end. 「最後まで歩き通した」 means you walked the whole way.

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜切る」 focuses on the result of finishing everything with nothing left (「使い切る」); 「〜通す」 focuses on the uninterrupted process from start to finish (「読み通す」).

similar.title: 〜を通して・〜を通じて
similar.explanation: Same origin: also from 「通す」 (to pass through). 「〜を通して」 follows a noun and means “by means of” or “throughout a period” (「一年を通して」); this pattern follows a verb masu-stem and means carrying an action through to the end.

formation: 「〜通す」 = verb masu-stem + 「通す」 (to pass something through). The image of 「通す」 is threading a line from one end to the other without a break. After a verb, it means running the action straight through from start to finish: 「読み通す」 = reading from the first page to the last. Because there can be no break in between, it carries a sense of will: not giving up, seeing it through (「やり通す」, 「守り通す」). The noun form 「〜通し」 turns this “without a break” into a state, meaning you keep doing the same thing: 「立ち通し」 (standing the whole time).

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. You do something and then leave it as it is, or the same state keeps going. It often shows annoyance.
connection: Verb masu-stem + っぱなし (だ／で／の + noun／にする)

senses.label: Left as is
senses.meaning: After an action, something that should be put back or finished is just left. It usually carries criticism: “leave ... on / open / out”.
senses.connection: Transitive verb masu-stem + っぱなし (開けっぱなし・出しっぱなし・つけっぱなし・置きっぱなし)
examples: I went out and left the window open.
Don't leave the water running.
I fell asleep with the TV on.

senses.label: Nonstop
senses.meaning: The same state continues for a long time without change: “... all the time, ... nonstop”. Often for negative or tiring things.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + っぱなし (立ちっぱなし・座りっぱなし・負けっぱなし・言われっぱなし)
examples: I was on my feet all day today, and my feet hurt.
This team has been losing nonstop lately.
She keeps criticizing me and I never get a word in. It's so frustrating.

notes: 「〜ておく」 means deliberately keeping something a certain way, while 「〜っぱなし」 means leaving something as it is when you should have dealt with it. They are opposites: 「窓を開けておいた」 means you left the window open on purpose (say, for air), while 「窓を開けっぱなしにした」 means you opened it and forgot to close it.
「〜っぱなし」 has a reproachful tone. Saying 「電気がつけっぱなしですよ」 to a superior or client sounds like you're scolding them. To point it out gently, say 「電気がついたままになっているようですが…」.
Add the small っ when connecting: 「開けっぱなし」, 「出しっぱなし」, not ✕「開けぱなし」 or ✕「開けてっぱなし」.
It is mostly negative. 「勝ちっぱなし」 and 「笑いっぱなし」 are possible, but for positively “keeping at something”, use 「〜続ける」.

daily.title: Nagging family
daily.description: A mom scolds her child for leaving the light on.
daily.example: You left the light on again!

daily.title: Complaining about work
daily.description: A store clerk says they stood all day.
daily.example: I was on my feet the whole shift at my part-time job.

daily.title: Tidying up
daily.description: A roommate leaves things lying around.
daily.example: Don't leave the laundry out, OK?

work.title: Office management
work.description: General affairs reminds staff to turn off equipment.
work.example: The projector in the meeting room was left on.

work.title: Health tip
work.description: Explaining the harm of sitting all day.
work.example: Jobs where you sit for long hours aren't good for your health.

etymology: It comes from 「放し」, the noun form of 「放す」 (let go). When it follows a verb masu-stem, a small 「っ」 is added, giving 「〜っぱなし」. Literally, “do it, then let it go (and leave it)”.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜たまま」 neutrally expresses that something stays as it was (「靴をはいたまま入る」); 「〜っぱなし」 stresses leaving something undealt with and carries dissatisfaction. The connection also differs: 「つけたまま」 uses the ta-form, 「つけっぱなし」 the masu-stem.

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (often compared): 「〜ておく」 deliberately keeps a state for some purpose, while 「〜っぱなし」 is leaving it be through carelessness. 「エアコンをつけておいた」 means you turned the AC on in advance; 「エアコンをつけっぱなしだった」 means you forgot to turn it off.

similar.title: 〜放題
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「放題」 and 「放し」 both use 「放」 (let go, leave to itself). 「〜放題」 means doing as you please without restraint (「食べ放題」, 「言いたい放題」); 「〜っぱなし」 means doing something and then walking away from it, or one state continuing on and on.

similar.title: 〜続ける
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: for continuation, 「〜続ける」 is neutral and usually means the subject actively keeps at something (「走り続ける」); 「〜っぱなし」 is usually an unwanted or passive continuation (「立ちっぱなし」, 「負けっぱなし」).

formation: 「〜っぱなし」 = verb masu-stem + 「放し」 (noun form of 「放す」, to let go, release). In the connection a small っ is inserted and 「はなし」 becomes 「ぱなし」, so it is written 「〜っぱなし」, or sometimes 「〜っ放し」. Literally it means “do something and then let go of it”: 「開けっぱなし」 = open it and let go → it stays open. “Letting go” means what should have been wrapped up wasn't, so it usually carries reproach or dissatisfaction. Highlighting the fact that the state is never interrupted after letting go gives the meaning “all the time, nonstop”: 「立ちっぱなし」, 「負けっぱなし」.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. An action has just been completed, so the thing or state is very fresh.
connection: Verb masu-stem + たて (の + noun／だ)

senses.label: Freshly made
senses.meaning: Food or the like has just been made and is fresh: “freshly ..., fresh from ...”. Usually 「〜たての + noun」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たての + noun (焼きたて・できたて・炊きたて・取れたて・搾りたて)
examples: Freshly baked bread is really delicious.
Please enjoy the dishes while they're fresh and hot.
We use freshly picked vegetables.

senses.label: Newly become
senses.meaning: A person has only just entered a role or state and isn't used to it yet: “new to ..., just ...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たて (生まれたて・入りたて・覚えたて・入社したて)
examples: Newborn babies are really tiny.
He just joined the company, so he isn't used to the work yet.
I tried speaking in the Japanese I had just learned.

notes: 「ペンキ塗りたて」 is a warning sign meaning “wet paint, do not touch”, not an advertisement boasting “freshly painted, brand-new”.
「〜たて」 only attaches to a small set of verbs that produce something new (焼く・作る・できる・取れる・生まれる・入社する, etc.) and can't be attached freely: ✕「読みたての本」→ ○「読んだばかりの本」.
To report that you just finished doing something, use 「〜たところ」 or 「〜たばかり」, not 「〜たて」: ✕「今、ご飯を食べたてです」→ ○「今、ご飯を食べたところです」.

daily.title: At a bakery
daily.description: A clerk recommends something to a customer.
daily.example: These are fresh out of the oven.

daily.title: Family dinner
daily.description: Calling everyone to eat the rice while it's hot.
daily.example: Freshly cooked rice is the best, isn't it?

daily.title: A paint sign
daily.description: A sign on a park bench.
daily.example: Wet paint. Please do not sit.

work.title: Introducing a newcomer
work.description: A senior employee tells a client about a new hire.
work.example: She just joined us, so we appreciate your patience with her.

work.title: Restaurant ad
work.description: Advertising copy for a restaurant.
work.example: Every morning we serve fresh fish delivered straight from the source.

etymology: It is generally thought to come from 「立て」, the masu-stem of 「立つ／立てる」, meaning something has just appeared or just begun. As a suffix, it is usually written in kana: 「たて」.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜たばかり」 uses the ta-form, works with almost any verb, and expresses the speaker's feeling that something happened “only a short time ago” (「日本に来たばかり」). 「〜たて」 uses the masu-stem, is limited to a few verbs, and stresses that something is “fresh, just made” (「焼きたてのパン」).

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜たところだ」 stresses the moment right after an action ended, and is mostly used to report your own actions (「今、着いたところです」). 「〜たて」 describes the fresh state of a thing or person, and isn't used to report on an action's progress.

formation: 「〜たて」 = verb masu-stem + 「たて」. 「たて」 is generally thought to come from the stem form of 「立つ」, meaning “just stood up, just appeared”. After a verb, it means “this action has just been completed and its result has just appeared”: 「焼きたて」 = just out of the oven. Because it focuses on a result that has just appeared, it almost always describes things or people (「〜たての + noun」), with a feel of “fresh, still warm, not yet experienced”. And because it is a fixed word-building element, it only pairs with verbs that create something new or a new status, such as baking, making, harvesting, being born, or joining a company.

meaning: Attached to a noun or verb masu-stem. It shows a slight (usually bad) tendency or feeling.
connection: Noun／verb masu-stem + 気味 (だ／で／の + noun)

senses.label: Body, mood
senses.meaning: Feeling “a bit ...” physically or emotionally. The degree is mild, and it is usually a bad state: “a touch of ..., a little ...”.
senses.connection: Noun／verb masu-stem + 気味 (風邪気味・疲れ気味・緊張気味・寝不足気味)
examples: I think I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll go to bed early tonight.
I've been a bit tired lately and have no energy.
He seemed a little nervous before the interview.

senses.label: Trend
senses.meaning: Something shows an undesirable tendency: “tending to ..., a bit ...”.
senses.connection: Noun／verb masu-stem + 気味 (遅れ気味・太り気味・不足気味・下がり気味)
examples: The construction is running slightly behind schedule.
I've been putting on a little weight lately.
We're a bit short-staffed, so everyone is busy.

notes: 「〜気味」 only means “a slight tendency toward...”, a mild degree: telling a doctor 「風邪気味です」 means “I feel like I'm coming down with a cold”, not “I have a cold”.
It is mostly used for bad tendencies; with positive words it sounds very unnatural: ✕「元気気味」, ✕「幸せ気味」.
「いい気味だ」 is read 「いいきみだ」 and means “serves you right”. It is gloating, and saying it to someone is very rude. 「気味が悪い」 (creepy) also has nothing to do with this pattern.
Commenting on someone's figure, as in 「太り気味ですね」, is very rude to say to their face in Japan. Saying it about yourself (「最近、太り気味で…」) is fine.

daily.title: Explaining how you feel
daily.description: Turning down a friend's dinner invitation.
daily.example: Sorry, I think I'm catching a cold, so I'll pass today.

daily.title: After a checkup
daily.description: Worrying about your weight.
daily.example: I haven't been getting much exercise lately, so I try to walk.

work.title: Project progress
work.description: Reporting a slight delay to your boss.
work.example: The schedule is running a little behind, so I'll make adjustments.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: A news report on the market.
work.example: Stock prices are trending slightly downward.

etymology: 「気味」 originally meant “feeling, sense”, like a hint of a smell or appearance. As a suffix, it came to mean “having a feeling of ..., slightly ...”, and the reading changed to 「ぎみ」.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜っぽい」 is casual and means “like..., has a feel of...”, and can be neutral too (「子供っぽい」, 「白っぽい」). 「〜気味」 specifically means “a slight (usually bad) tendency”, and often describes health or situations. 「風邪っぽい」 and 「風邪気味」 are close in meaning; the latter is more formal.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜がち」 expresses a tendency for something to happen “often, repeatedly” (「休みがち」); 「〜気味」 expresses being “slightly” in some state right now (「疲れ気味」). The first is about frequency; the second is about degree.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「眠そうだ」 is a guess based on appearance, “looks sleepy”, and is mostly used about other people. 「〜気味」 describes a state that really is “a bit...”, and is often used about yourself or objective situations (「寝不足気味だ」).

similar.title: 〜傾向がある・〜傾向にある
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜傾向がある」 is written style and refers to a long-term, overall trend (「若者は新聞を読まない傾向がある」). 「〜気味」 is conversational and usually refers to a temporary, mild state right now (「最近、寝不足気味だ」).

formation: 「〜気味」 = noun / verb masu-stem + 「気味」. 「気味」 is made of 「気」 (air, feeling) and 「味」 (taste, look), and originally meant “a certain air or feeling”. Attached to another word, it means “having an air of...”, in other words “looking slightly...”: 「風邪気味」 = carrying an air of a cold. Since it is only an “air”, the degree is mild and it's not fully the case. And since people usually say it when they notice their health or a situation is “a bit off”, it mainly attaches to negative words. As a suffix, its reading becomes voiced: 「ぎみ」.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. It is psychologically hard to do or accept something. It has a fairly formal, written tone.
connection: Verb masu-stem + がたい (in kanji: 〜難い)

senses.label: Hard to accept
senses.meaning: Even if you want to, it is emotionally hard to accept or do: “hard to ..., can hardly ...”. Often with 「信じる」, 「許す」, 「理解する」, 「認める」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + がたい (信じがたい・許しがたい・理解しがたい・受け入れがたい)
examples: It's hard to believe he would do something like that.
This is an unforgivable act.
That explanation is hard to understand.

senses.label: Rare, unforgettable
senses.meaning: Some words are fixed expressions. 「得がたい」 means “rare, precious” and 「忘れがたい」 means “unforgettable”. They usually modify nouns and are positive.
senses.connection: 得がたい・忘れがたい・離れがたい + noun
examples: Studying abroad turned out to be an invaluable experience.
I have many unforgettable memories.

notes: 「〜がたい」 means it is psychologically hard to accept or to think that way. It is not used for difficulty due to ability or physical factors: ✕「この漢字は書きがたい」→ ○「この漢字は書きにくい」.
It is formal and literary. Saying 「信じがたい」 in everyday conversation sounds stiff; in speech, people usually say 「信じられない」.
「ありがたい」 (grateful, welcome) comes from 「有り難い」 (rare to exist) and is now an independent adjective, so don't read it as “hard to have”. For “hard to obtain”, say 「得がたい」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Seeing a report on a shocking incident.
daily.example: I can hardly believe something like this happened.

daily.title: Graduation farewell
daily.description: Telling classmates you don't want to part.
daily.example: I really don't want to leave you all.

work.title: Official statement
work.description: A company issues a statement on misconduct.
work.example: This misconduct is absolutely unacceptable.

work.title: Evaluating staff
work.description: HR praises an employee as rare talent.
work.example: He is a truly valuable person to have.

etymology: 「がたい」 is the adjective 「難い (かたい)」, meaning “difficult”, voiced when used as a suffix. So 「〜がたい」 literally means “hard to ...”.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜にくい」 is the most neutral and covers physical, ability-related, and psychological difficulty (「書きにくいペン」). 「〜がたい」 is only for things that are psychologically hard to accept or do, and has a strong written tone (「許しがたい」, 「信じがたい」).

similar.title: 〜づらい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜づらい」 leans conversational and means the person doing it feels uncomfortable or awkward (「言いづらい」). 「〜がたい」 leans written and means it is hard to do for reasons of logic or emotion (「理解しがたい」).

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜かねる」 means you can't do something because of your position or circumstances, and is often used to decline politely (「お引き受けしかねます」). 「〜がたい」 is mostly used to evaluate something as “hard to...”, and generally isn't used to turn down a request.

formation: 「〜がたい」 = verb masu-stem + 「がたい」. 「がたい」 is the adjective 「難い（かたい）」 voiced when used as a suffix. 「難い」 originally means “difficult”, so the whole structure means “doing (something) is difficult”. Since 「難い」 is an old, elegant literary word, 「〜がたい」 inherits that written, formal tone. It mostly pairs with mental verbs like 「信じる・許す・理解する・忘れる」, so the difficulty mainly comes from inner reluctance to accept, not from lack of ability.

meaning: Attached to a verb masu-stem. Doing something feels hard or uncomfortable, physically or emotionally. Fairly casual.
connection: Verb masu-stem + づらい (in kanji: 〜辛い)

senses.label: Emotionally hard
senses.meaning: It feels hard to do because you're worried about the other person or feel awkward: “hard to bring yourself to ..., awkward to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + づらい (言いづらい・頼みづらい・断りづらい・聞きづらい)
examples: It's hard to ask a senior colleague to lend me money.
He looks busy, so I feel bad asking him to do it.
It's hard to turn down a friend's invitation.

senses.label: Physically hard
senses.meaning: Doing it feels tiring or uncomfortable for the body: “hard to ..., a pain to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + づらい (歩きづらい・読みづらい・見づらい・食べづらい)
examples: These shoes are hard to walk in.
The screen is dark, so it's hard to see.
The letters were small and hard to read.

notes: 「〜づらい」 expresses the doer's subjective discomfort or awkwardness, and isn't used for objective properties of things: ✕「この紙は燃えづらい」→ ○「この紙は燃えにくい」.
The standard spelling is 「〜づらい」 (from 「辛い」). 「〜ずらい」 is a common misspelling and looks unprofessional in formal documents.
「ちょっと言いづらいんですが…」 is a common lead-in Japanese people use before raising something hard to say (a refusal, a complaint). It is more tactful than coming straight out with it.
On its own, 「辛い」 is read 「つらい」 (painful) or 「からい」 (spicy); after a verb it is read 「づらい」, never ✕「からい」.

daily.title: Declining an invitation
daily.description: Friends discuss how to skip a party.
daily.example: They went out of their way to invite me, so it's hard to say no.

daily.title: Tiny print
daily.description: An older person reads a medicine leaflet.
daily.example: The print in the instructions is too small to read easily.

daily.title: Awkward mood
daily.description: Feeling awkward after a fight.
daily.example: Since our fight, it's been hard to talk to him.

work.title: A tactful request
work.description: Bringing up something awkward with a boss.
work.example: I'm sorry to have to ask, but could you extend the delivery date?

work.title: Improving the workplace
work.description: Discussing how hard it is for staff to take leave.
work.example: I want to change the atmosphere that makes it hard to take time off.

etymology: It comes from the adjective 「辛い (つらい)」, meaning “painful, hard to bear”. After a verb it is voiced to 「づらい」, literally “painful to do”.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜にくい」 is objective and neutral and can describe things or phenomena (「燃えにくい素材」). 「〜づらい」 is subjective and stresses the doer's physical or mental discomfort (「足が痛くて歩きづらい」).

similar.title: 〜がたい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜がたい」 is written style and means hard to accept for reasons of logic or emotion (「信じがたい」, 「許しがたい」). 「〜づらい」 is conversational and means uncomfortable or awkward to do (「言いづらい」, 「頼みづらい」).

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「言いづらい」 means you yourself find it hard to bring up; 「〜かねる」 means you can't agree because of your position, and is mostly used to decline politely (「お答えしかねます」). When declining a client, use 「〜かねます」; 「〜づらいです」 makes it sound like mere personal feelings.

formation: 「〜づらい」 = verb masu-stem + 「づらい」. 「づらい」 comes from the adjective 「辛い（つらい）」, originally meaning “painful, hard to bear”; after a verb it becomes voiced as 「づらい」, literally “painful to do”. Precisely because it comes from a personal feeling of pain, the difficulty in 「〜づらい」 always starts from the doer's body or mind: 「言いづらい」 is feeling uneasy when speaking up, and 「歩きづらい」 is your body hurting as you walk. This is the most fundamental difference from 「〜にくい」, which describes objective properties.

meaning: Attached to a noun. Something is designed or made specifically for a certain group of people or target.

senses.label: Aimed at people
senses.meaning: Designed or made with a certain group in mind: “for ..., aimed at ...”. The focus is on the maker's intention.
senses.connection: Noun (group of people) + 向けの + noun／向けに (子供向け・初心者向け・若者向け)
examples: This is a children's program.
It's a book written in plain language for beginners.
This magazine is aimed at young women.

senses.label: Aimed at a region
senses.meaning: Targeting a certain region or market. Common with exports and services.
senses.connection: Place／market + 向け (海外向け・アジア向け・国内向け)
examples: We are developing products for overseas markets.
This car was built for the Asian market.

notes: 「〜向け」 means “made specifically for...” (the maker's intention), while 「〜向き」 means “suited to...” (the thing's own nature): 「子供向けの本」 is a book written specially for children, and 「子供向きの本」 is a book that suits children.
「〜向け」 attaches directly to a noun, without 「に」: ✕「子供に向けの番組」→ ○「子供向けの番組」. Adding 「に」 makes it a different pattern, 「〜に向けて」 (toward, in preparation for).
「海外向け」 and 「アジア市場向け」 mean sold or shipped to that place, not “facing in that direction”.

daily.title: Choosing a book
daily.description: Looking for a book for a child at a bookstore.
daily.example: Where are the picture encyclopedias for elementary school kids?

daily.title: Signing up for a class
daily.description: A friend recommends a beginner class.
daily.example: There's a yoga class for beginners.

work.title: Product development
work.description: Discussing target customers in a meeting.
work.example: We planned this new product for older people.

work.title: Investor relations
work.description: A company announces materials for investors.
work.example: We will hold a briefing session for investors.

etymology: It comes from the masu-stem of the verb 「向ける」 (turn something toward). “Pointing something at someone” came to mean “making it with someone as the target”.

similar.title: 〜向き
similar.explanation: Same origin (similar meaning): both come from “facing”. 「〜向け」 stresses that the maker targeted a certain group and made it “specifically for” them; 「〜向き」 stresses that the thing itself “suits” a certain group. 「初心者向けの講座」 is a course set up specially for beginners; 「初心者向きの講座」 is a course that also suits beginners.

similar.title: 〜に向けて
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「向ける」. 「〜に向けて」 has 「に」 and means an action directed at someone (「国民に向けて話す」) or preparing toward a goal (「試合に向けて練習する」); 「〜向け」 attaches directly to a noun and expresses a category, “aimed at...”.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both 「子供のための本」 and 「子供向けの本」 are possible. 「〜のため」 stresses purpose, doing it for the other person's good; 「〜向け」 stresses the target group set when designing it, and sounds more like a product category label.

formation: 「〜向け」 = noun + 「向け」 (the stem form of the transitive verb 「向ける」, used as a noun). 「向ける」 means “to point something toward”, so there is always someone doing the pointing. That's why 「〜向け」 implies the maker's intention: products or programs are made “pointed toward” a certain group. 「子供向け」 = the maker aimed it at children. As a noun, it can stick right onto another noun as a category label, use 「の」 to modify nouns (「若者向けの雑誌」), and 「に」 to work adverbially (「初心者向けに説明する」). When the target is a region, “pointing toward” becomes the direction of export or shipping (「海外向け」).

meaning: Attached to a noun. It means facing a certain direction, or being suitable for certain people or a certain use.

senses.label: Facing
senses.meaning: Facing a certain direction: “...-facing”. Common with houses and directions.
senses.connection: Direction noun + 向き (南向き・東向き・横向き・上向き)
examples: South-facing rooms are bright and warm.
Sleeping on your side is comfortable.

senses.label: Suitable for
senses.meaning: Something is by nature suitable for certain people or situations, though not necessarily made for them: “good for ..., suited to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + 向き (初心者向き・子供向き・夏向き)／不向き
examples: This course is good for beginners.
This dish isn't spicy, so it's good for kids.
He may not be cut out for sales.

senses.label: Positive, negative
senses.meaning: 「前向き」 means positive, forward-looking; 「後ろ向き」 means negative, backward-looking. They have become fixed na-adjectives.
senses.connection: 前向き・後ろ向き + な／に
examples: Let's think positively about everything.
Stop thinking so negatively.

notes: In business, when you hear 「前向きに検討します」, it literally means “we'll consider it positively”, but it is often just polite talk and is not a yes. Don't assume the deal is done.
「〜向き」 means “suited to”, while 「〜向け」 means “made specifically for”. Don't mix them up: 「子供向きの料理」 is food that suits children, and 「子供向けの料理」 is food made specially for children.
For “not suited”, say 「不向き」 or 「向いていない」: ✕「この仕事は私に向きではない」→ ○「この仕事は私には不向きだ」／「私には向いていない」.
To say a person is suited to a profession, the verb form 「〜に向いている」 is usual: 「彼は教師に向いている」, not ✕「彼は教師に向きだ」.

daily.description: Telling a real estate agent what you want.
daily.example: I'm looking for a sunny, south-facing room.

daily.title: Cheering up a friend
daily.description: Encouraging a friend who is down.
daily.example: Don't be down. Let's stay positive!

daily.example: This is a cool fabric that's good for summer.

work.example: He has a personality suited to detailed work.

work.title: Business reply
work.description: Giving a client a positive response to a proposal.
work.example: We will give your proposal positive consideration.

etymology: It comes from 「向き」, the masu-stem of the verb 「向く」 (face). Facing in space came to mean “leaning toward, suited to” in nature.

similar.title: 〜向け
similar.explanation: Same origin (similar meaning): both come from “facing”. 「〜向き」 stresses that the thing itself “suits” a certain group (「初心者向きのコース」); 「〜向け」 stresses that the maker targeted a certain group and made it “specifically for” them (「初心者向けのコース」).

similar.title: 〜に向かって
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「向く」. 「〜に向かって」 means an action moving in a direction or facing someone (「海に向かって叫ぶ」); the 「〜向き」 in 「南向き」 expresses a fixed orientation of a thing.

similar.title: 〜に合わせて・〜に合った
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜に合った」 means “matching, fitting”, focusing on whether things match (「自分に合った仕事」); 「〜向き」 means suited to a certain type of person and is often used as a category judgment (「初心者向き」).

formation: 「〜向き」 = noun + 「向き」 (the stem form of the intransitive verb 「向く」, used as a noun). 「向く」 means “to face a direction on its own”, with no outside agent, so 「〜向き」 describes a thing's own orientation or nature: 「南向きの部屋」 = the room itself faces south. From spatially “facing someone”, it extends to “by nature leaning toward, suited to someone”: 「子供向き」 = naturally appealing to children. Extended further to attitudes, it gives 「前向き」 (positive) and 「後ろ向き」 (negative). It contrasts with 「〜向け」, which comes from a transitive verb and implies someone deliberately pointing it, and that is the difference between “suited to” and “made specifically for”.
